title: A Terminal for the Horizon Revisited
premise: Ines Halloran, the fourth clone of a murdered beacon-keeper, has spent his short life maintaining a relay nobody will claim, haunted by fragments of his predecessor's unsolved death. When every child in the colony begins dreaming the same dream — a voice counting down from inside dead space — Ines realizes the signal is not a distress call but an invitation, and that the original Ines answered it once. Racing a failing reactor and the colony's council, who want the relay silenced, he travels to the horizon terminal with a stowaway girl who dreams loudest of all. There he finds the original alive in the signal's archive, learns the murder was staged by those who feared contact, and must choose between preserving his borrowed identity or merging with the accumulated selves before him. He chooses neither: he broadcasts the truth, frees the children's dream, and returns as someone new — the first Ines who is only himself.
about_author: Mirabel Villalobos is a former radio telescope technician who spent six years at remote listening stations before turning to fiction full-time. She writes science fiction about lonely infrastructure and the people who keep it running.

chapters.title: The Man Who Was Filed Under Maintenance
chapters.summary: Ines Halloran's POV. A routine day tending the beacon: coolant flushes, log entries signed with a name that legally belongs to three dead men. He catalogs the original's belongings, including a locked case he's never opened. Emotional beat: quiet loneliness disguised as competence.

chapters.title: Children Who Dream in Unison
chapters.summary: Colony teacher Amara Osei's POV. Her students fall asleep mid-lesson and wake reciting identical phrases: a countdown, a door, a woman made of static. The council dismisses it as mass hysteria. Amara notices one phrase matches beacon maintenance codes. Beat: unease blooming into wonder.

chapters.title: Log Entries Signed by Dead Men
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Auditing old beacon records, he finds entries dated after each clone's death — all in his own handwriting style. The last entry reads: 'They'll send another me. Tell him about the dream.' Beat: dread; the inheritance is not property but a message.

chapters.title: The Council Wants Silence
chapters.summary: Councilor Davor Reyes's POV. Reyes argues the relay is an unlicensed liability and moves to decommission it, revealing the colony charter forbids contact with dead space. Privately, he burns a file on the original Ines's murder. Beat: cold institutional fear hiding guilt.

chapters.title: A Girl Who Dreams Loudest
chapters.summary: Nine-year-old Sefa Ilic's POV. She describes the dream precisely — a corridor, a heartbeat, a name being erased letter by letter — and draws the beacon's interior she's never seen. She runs away from home toward the relay. Beat: innocence as urgency.

chapters.title: Stowaway
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Preparing to investigate the signal alone, he discovers Sefa hiding in his supply sled. She recites the countdown's current number; it matches the reactor's fault log exactly. He can't turn back in time to return her. Beat: reluctant responsibility becoming tenderness.

chapters.title: What the Original Left Locked
chapters.summary: Ines's POV, en route. He finally opens the locked case: the original's journal, evidence of sabotage in the reactor, and a photograph of two people — the original and Councilor Reyes, younger, arm in arm. Beat: betrayal reframing everything; duty was never neutral.

chapters.title: Dead Space Is Not Empty
chapters.summary: Sefa's POV. Outside the colony's sensor range, the ship's instruments fail but Sefa navigates flawlessly by the dream. They pass derelict probes, all pointed inward, all ancient. She says the voice sounds 'like someone practicing being a person.' Beat: awe and mounting strangeness.

chapters.title: Interrogation of a Ghost
chapters.summary: Amara's POV. Questioned by Reyes about the children, she stalls, then breaks into the council archive and finds the original Ines's murder report — closed in four days, no body ever recovered. Beat: righteous anger; the found-family thread tightens around the truth.

chapters.title: The Relay at the Edge
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. They reach the horizon terminal: intact, powered, older than the colony. Inside, the air hums with the countdown. Sefa walks straight to a console and places her hand on it like greeting someone. Beat: threshold terror; arrival as homecoming.

chapters.title: Voices in the Archive
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. The terminal speaks with the original's voice: the first Ines discovered the signal years ago, faked his own death when Reyes moved to destroy the relay, and uploaded his memories into the beacon's buffer. Every clone since has been slowly receiving them. Beat: identity crisis — Ines is both heir and hostage.

chapters.title: Four Days, No Body
chapters.summary: Reyes's POV. Flashback chapter: young Reyes and the original Ines were co-founders; when Ines chose contact over protocol, Reyes reported him dead to protect the colony's charter — and himself. His guilt has calcified into policy. Beat: tragic antagonist sympathy.

chapters.title: Countdown Logic
chapters.summary: Sefa's POV. She explains the dream isn't a warning — the countdown is the archive's memory degrading, the original dissolving. The children heard it because dying minds broadcast loudest. If it reaches zero, everything he knew dies with him. Beat: heartbreak; a child carrying adult grief.

chapters.title: The Colony Comes for the Beacon
chapters.summary: Amara's POV. Reyes dispatches a shutdown team; Amara, having found the falsified report, races to warn Ines by the only channel left — the beacon itself, feeding coordinates into the dream. The children wake speaking her message. Beat: solidarity; found family acting as one organism.

chapters.title: Merge or Remain
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. The archive offers him total integration — every prior self's memories, skills, and the answer to his own origin. But integration means the person he's become ends. Sefa tells him the dream showed her 'a man choosing which man to be.' Beat: the book's thematic crux.

chapters.title: Shutdown Team
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. The council team arrives; their leader is a clone too — of Reyes's late partner, grown for loyalty. Ines shows her the journal instead of fighting. She hesitates as the reactor's countdown syncs audibly with the archive's. Beat: tension peaking; enemies recognizing themselves.

chapters.title: Love Against Duty
chapters.summary: Reyes's POV. Confronted via live feed by the original's voice — patient, unresentful — Reyes's forty-year edifice collapses. He orders the team to stand down, then confesses publicly to the colony. Beat: catharsis through surrender; love outlasting ideology.

chapters.title: The Broadcast
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Instead of merging, Ines does something new: he opens the archive to everyone, letting the original's memories disperse across the colony's network rather than die or dominate one mind. The countdown stops — not saved, but shared. Beat: triumphant subversion of the binary choice.

chapters.title: What the Children Remember
chapters.summary: Sefa's POV. The dream fades, leaving warmth instead of dread. The children retain fragments — languages, star charts, the original's laugh. Sefa keeps one thing privately: how to say goodbye. Beat: bittersweet wonder; grief metabolized into inheritance.

chapters.title: Homecoming of a New Man
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Returning to the colony, Ines petitions to change his legal name — not to erase the lineage but to end it: he will be the last and only Ines Halloran. Amara meets the sled at the gate. Beat: quiet joy; identity claimed rather than assigned.

chapters.title: A Terminal for the Horizon
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Months later, the relay is repurposed as a school annex; children learn from the dispersed archive under supervision. Ines maintains it still — but now people remember why. He signs his log with his own hand, meaning only himself. Beat: peace earned, purpose renewed.

chapters.title: Signal, Answered
chapters.summary: Epilogue, rotating POVs — Ines, Sefa, Amara, one line each. Deep in dead space, something ancient receives the colony's first outbound transmission and, for the first time in centuries, answers. Final beat: the horizon is no longer terminal; it's a beginning.
